items.title: 5 Key Risks in the 10-Year Retirement Gap
items.summary:
If you're like most people nearing or in retirement , you've spent 20- to 30-plus years building your retirement savings. You've made sacrifices, saved diligently, invested consistently and watched your portfolio grow. 

But how many of us think about preparing for the next chapter? There's a transition on the horizon that doesn't happen automatically when you punch out for the last time and enter retirement. 

That transition should begin years before your final workday. The decisions you make in the five to 10 years before you retire, and in the first five years after, could shape your financial future more than any other period of your life.

I call this stretch of time the retirement danger gap, and it deserves far more attention than most people give it. It's the bridge between two very different phases: Growing your wealth and living on it while making sure it lasts. 

The ripple effect The gap shows up in the decisions you make during these years and in how those decisions ripple through the rest of your retirement . Making them without a trusted professional by your side can be the difference between a retirement that thrives and one that struggles.

When you were still working, you had two advantages: Time and paychecks. If the market had a rough spot when you were 40 years old, you could shrug it off, knowing you had plenty of time to recover any losses.

items.title: Financial Adviser Fees: The View From a Consumer Advocate
items.summary:
One of the biggest myths about financial adviser fees is that the amount of money you have to invest drives the fee you'll pay for the advice. 

It's true that most advisers prefer to charge based on a percentage of your assets they manage, but the size of your portfolio doesn't necessarily reflect how much financial and tax planning you need or how complicated your financial life may be.

Someone with $500,000 in savings, several retirement accounts, rental properties and a complicated tax situation may need substantially more planning than someone with $2 million invested in a simple portfolio of index funds. 

The true story about adviser fees is that the price should reflect the work involved, not simply the size of your portfolio. Before comparing fees , you need to understand what you want an adviser to accomplish and what kind of relationship makes sense for you.

Different needs call for different kinds of advice One of the most important developments in financial advice is that consumers now have more choices in how they work with qualified, fee-only fiduciary advisers .

items.title: 5 Tax Traps That Cost Retirees When Downsizing
items.summary:
While many retirees are staying put in 2026, some plan to trade their larger homestead for simpler, easier-to-manage space.

According to Freddie Mac research , 66% of Baby Boomer homeowners (aged 62 to 80 in 2026) who are planning to move say they intend to downsize, joining the 36% of Boomer movers who have already scaled back.

Downsizing may offer some clear perks, like moving closer to family, ditching yard work, or freeing up home equity. Yet for longtime homeowners sitting on decades of appreciated value, the biggest financial hurdle may lie in the U.S. tax code.

That's because IRS rules hold several quiet traps that can turn a familial home sale into an unexpected tax bill . For instance, claiming a home office deduction years ago can erase tens of thousands of dollars in tax-free capital gains.

So before you put a "for sale" sign in your yard, watch out for these five hidden downsizing tax traps in 2026.

1. Missing the two-year deadline for surviving spouses 

(Image credit: Getty Images) Losing a spouse is overwhelming, and rushing into a move is often the last thing on a grieving partner's mind. Yet waiting too long to sell can unfortunately trigger what some tax pros call the " widow's tax penalty ."

When married couples sell a primary residence, federal rules typically allow a capital gains tax exclusion of up to $500,000. Many retirees assume they can wait several years after a spouse passes away to downsize, not realizing half of that tax shield expires on a deadline. Under IRS rules , an unmarried surviving spouse only keeps the full $500,000 home sale…

items.title: The 5-Year Retirement Shortfall Awaiting the Average American
items.summary:
Planning for only average conditions, with little room for error, can sink any journey. Sometimes tragically so, as with the ill-fated Robert Falcon Scott expedition racing to be first to the South Pole. Beset by blizzards and low on fuel, Scott and his crew perished only 11 miles short of their next supply station.

Many Americans may be facing their own devastating shortfall in the journey known as retirement, according to a recent survey. The life insurance company Ethos asked 1,000 Americans about their retirement savings and found the average American wants to live to 88 but says their savings can only support them to 83 .

The good news is that this five-year retirement gap between lifespan and savings isn't set in stone. Experts suggest a mix of moves — some that grow your assets, others that make them last longer — can help keep your savings from running out before you do.

Here are five key strategies to get started.

1. Plan for living longer than you think The saying, "no one wants to be average," could actually be the perfect attitude for your retirement plan.

As Matthew Chancey, CFP® and founder of Tax Alpha Companies , points out, "The real shortfall usually starts with planning to the average." He explains that Social Security Administration actuaries estimate a man who is 65 today will live to about 83, on average, and a woman to about 86. Because those are averages, roughly half of people live longer. So a plan built to the average age is a plan that runs out about half the time.

That's why some advisers suggest building a plan around living to 90 or…
items.t: The 5-Year Retirement Shortfall Awaiting the Average American

items.title: The Hardest Retirement Skill: Spending What You Saved
items.summary:
For the 30 or 40 years or more of our working lives, the instructions are straightforward: Save. Invest. Max out what you can. Don't touch the retirement accounts. Watch the balances grow.

Then retirement arrives and the instructions suddenly reverse: Now start spending the money.

For disciplined savers, that shift can be harder than it sounds. Watching a balance decline can feel like failure, even when spending that money is exactly what your financial plan says you can afford to do. Spending is exactly what you've been saving for.

A successful retirement plan gives you the financial strategy to build your retirement savings and the confidence to spend that money so you can enjoy this chapter of your life. Your nest egg may be ready, but your mindset might need to catch up. Here's how to get in the right retirement spending headspace.

1. Start with your life, not your number If someone told me, "I have $1 million saved , so I'm ready to retire," my response would be, "Tell me about your life, not just your account balances." 

A number is just a number. What you really need to know is what you want your money to do for you. Money is a tool.

items.title: Waiting Until Your 70s for RMDs Can Spring a Pricey Tax Surprise
items.summary:
Required minimum distributions (RMDs) have a way of feeling like a problem for later. You are not required to take them yet, the account is growing nicely, and there is always next year to think about it. 

That comfort is exactly the trap. The cost of treating RMDs as a future concern is not paid when they begin. It is paid in the years you spent ignoring them, when you could have been acting and chose to wait. 

By the time the distributions arrive, the most valuable planning years are already behind you.

What RMDs actually are Once you reach a certain age, the IRS stops letting your tax-deferred accounts grow untouched. You must begin withdrawing a calculated amount each year from accounts like traditional IRAs and 401(k)s , whether you need the money or not, and each withdrawal is taxed as ordinary income. 

For 2026, the age at which RMDs generally begin is 73. The amount is determined by your account balance and an IRS life expectancy factor , and it rises as a percentage of the balance as you age.

The penalty for getting it wrong is steep. Miss an RMD and the shortfall can be hit with a penalty of 25%, reduced to 10% if you correct it promptly. That alone is reason enough to take them seriously. 

But the larger cost is not the penalty. It is what compounds quietly in the years before RMDs ever start.

items.title: Year-End Oil and Gas Investing to Lower Your 2026 Tax Bill
items.summary:
By the time fall rolls around, most business owners and high-income professionals have a pretty good idea of how their year is going to turn out. If business has been good and they've had a sizable bonus or an unexpected raise, they may also be looking at a larger tax bill than they originally planned.

That's usually when the phone starts ringing. People want to know whether there's anything they can do before December 31 to reduce what they'll owe in April. 

I've been in the oil and gas business for more than 35 years, and one of the things I often discuss with investors is how direct ownership in oil and gas wells may fit into their overall tax planning .

Most people know that oil and gas investments can offer tax advantages, but they don't always understand where those benefits came from or how they work. And with year-end rapidly approaching, understanding the difference between making an investment and qualifying for a deduction becomes especially important.

A tax benefit that's been around for more than 100 years The federal government has recognized the cost and risk of developing domestic oil and gas resources for more than a century. In fact, the tax treatment of intangible drilling costs dates back to the early years of the federal income tax system in 1913 and was later incorporated into federal law in 1954.

items.title: How to Manage Sudden Wealth: An Expert Guide
items.summary:
Receiving an unexpected amount of money can feel like the solution to all of life's financial challenges. Whether sudden wealth comes from an inheritance, a legal settlement, a work bonus or the lottery, there will be plenty of ways to use it. 

According to Empower , 65% of Americans say they'd save or invest a financial windfall and 52% say they'd use it to pay off debt. But however it's used, a sudden influx of money can be an emotional experience. Making decisions too quickly can impact your lifestyle and ongoing expenses, family relationships and boundaries, financial vulnerability and long-term financial security. 

Before making a major purchase, donation or investment, pause to consider how the windfall fits into your financial plan.

Your first move? Do nothing After a financial windfall , the first step might be to do nothing at all. Unless there's a financial emergency, major decisions don't need to be made right away. 

In the meantime, the money can be temporarily placed somewhere safe, such as a money market account, to allow time to evaluate the situation. This can be especially helpful with an inheritance, which might come while you're processing or grieving.

items.title: Is Your Homeowners Insurance Stuck in 1995?
items.summary:
Quick, which part of the U.S. gets natural disasters?

If you answered that hurricanes belong to Florida, wildfires to California and tornadoes to Kansas, congratulations, you have a perfectly good map of the situation before 1995. Now, fold it up and put it in the glove box next to the Thomas Guide.

That map is out of date. Like, ridiculously out of date, and our changing climate is loading the dice for bigger fires, heavier rain and longer heat waves, and it is doing it in places where you used to hear, "That doesn't happen here." Yes, that includes where you live. 

Check out some of the clips I've put on X and you'll see.

But don't take my word for it. Let's look at what has actually happened, followed by what you can do about it.

What we've been through recently In January 2025, wildfires tore through Los Angeles , killing at least 29 people and destroying or damaging more than 14,000 structures. I know this one personally because hundreds of my office's clients lost their homes. 

Scientists at World Weather Attribution found that a warming climate made the hot, dry, windy conditions behind those fires about 35% more likely. It was more like a tsunami fire than a wildfire.

items.title: Ask the Editor: Questions on Investments and Year-End Tax Planning
items.summary:
Each week in our Ask the Tax Editor series, Joy Taylor, The Kiplinger Tax Letter editor, answers questions on topics submitted by readers. This week, she's looking at four tax questions from readers on year-end tax planning strategies involving taxable investment accounts. ( Get a free issue of The Kiplinger Tax Letter or subscribe .) 

1. Tax-loss harvesting Question: I have lots of capital gains in my taxable investment account this year. My financial advisor suggested I sell some stocks that have gone down in value to minimize the tax hit. Is this a good tax move? 

Joy Taylor: Tax-loss harvesting (or capital-loss harvesting) is a popular way for investors to lower their federal income tax bills. The strategy involves selling stocks or other securities in your taxable investment accounts that have declined in value for the purpose of generating capital losses to offset capital gains from the sales of winners that you have sold during the year. Investors commonly do this closer to the end of the year, when they have a better idea of the amount of capital gains they will have.

If you are planning to sell stock you own at a loss to offset capital gains and then buy the same stock back soon thereafter, watch out for the wash-sale rule . You can’t deduct a capital loss from a sale of securities if you buy substantially identical securities up to 30 days before or after the sale. The recognized loss isn’t gone forever; it’s only suspended. That’s because the loss is added to the tax basis of your replacement securities.

The first, Your Diversified ETF Isn't as Diversified as You Think , examined how popular ETFs concentrate exposure to the AI capital spending cycle; the second, AI Is a Supply Chain Rather Than an Industry: Here's Why , mapped the supply chain layers behind that spending; the third, How to Manage the 4 Risks Hiding Inside Every AI-Heavy Portfolio , examined the risks facing the buildout itself. 

A new frontier AI model now reaches the market every few weeks. No hospital system, manufacturer, bank or retailer refreshes its production technology stack on that schedule, and none ever will.

That mismatch is not a minor operational footnote. It is a structural risk sitting underneath the valuation of nearly every company in the AI supply chain, because those valuations assume enterprise revenue will arrive on the same clock as model releases. It won't.

Two clocks running at different speeds Model providers compete on speed. The frontier model release cadence compressed dramatically through 2025 and into 2026: Labs that once shipped a major model roughly every six months moved to a pace of multiple substantive releases per week by early 2026, with one industry tracker counting more than a dozen meaningful frontier launches in the first quarter alone. 

A separate count found five major model launches or availability milestones in a single 16-day window in July 2026.

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

items.title: How Volunteering Builds Workplace Empathy
items.summary:
In more than 35 years managing people and culture, most recently as chief operating officer at Affinity Federal Credit Union, I've learned that the qualities that make someone good at serving members rarely start in an office. 

Empathy, patience and the instinct to listen before reacting usually are intangibles that develop somewhere else first, and then they show up at work.

A credit union runs on members trusting that the person helping them actually understands their situation. That kind of understanding is hard to teach in a training room. It's much easier to build in the middle of a real situation, with a real person, where there's no script to fall back on.

What a workshop can't recreate There's a difference between describing empathy in a session and actually experiencing it. A training module can explain active listening. It can't put someone in front of a stranger whose life looks nothing like their own and force them to figure out, in real time, what that person actually needs. But hands-on community service does exactly that.

I've watched employees come back from a volunteer project and engage differently almost immediately. They ask more questions before jumping to a solution, notice hesitation or frustration faster, and listen more than they used to.

We're in a whole new world this time

A lot has changed in the 13 years since GTA 5, which means players get a much improved experience. The graphics are dramatically sharper and more lifelike, and the gameplay feels more dynamic. items.title: 4 Ways Generational Wealth Goes Beyond Money
items.summary:
What is generational wealth ? We often think about it in terms of money: A person or family has generational wealth when they have enough to pass on from one generation to the next — and this is true. 

But a family's legacy includes more than money. It also includes the assets that help the next generation build a truly wealthy life.

With that, here are four assets — beyond money — that parents can pass on to their children, and practical ways to get started.

1. Health Parents can pass on health by modeling healthy habits while sharing family health history. The next generation benefits from seeing how to manage diet and stress, and from knowing which hereditary risks to be aware of.

The everyday angle: Share healthy habits, visibly and vocally. Invite your kids to cook a healthy meal with you, and feel free to process out loud: "I'm feeling stressed, so I'm going for a long walk after dinner." Share your family health history with your adult children, including major conditions on either side of the family and at what age they appeared.

The financial angle: You might walk your young adult through your health insurance policy, explaining premiums, deductibles and out-of-pocket costs. Share how you balance coverage and costs, so they can also make informed choices.

items.title: Which Types of ETFs Belong in a Taxable Brokerage Account?
items.summary:
An ordinary taxable brokerage account may lack the tax advantages of a Roth IRA or a 401(k) , but it beats both handily when it comes to flexibility. There are no annual contribution limits, income restrictions on eligibility or age-based withdrawal rules.

So you can deposit and withdraw your money whenever you choose, making accounts with brokers and trading platforms useful for financial goals that don't necessarily revolve around retirement. But this flexibility means you must account for taxes.

Investment returns in a brokerage account can receive different tax treatment depending on their source. Indeed, you may encounter short- and long-term capital gains , non-qualified and qualified dividends , ordinary interest income and return of capital.

These aren't all taxed at the same rate, and depending on the investment and where you live, they can create liabilities at both the federal and state levels. Providers of exchange-traded funds ( ETFs ) are well aware of this, which helps explain the increasingly diverse roster of funds designed to defer or minimize specific forms of tax drag.

Some accomplish this through the securities they hold, while others employ specialized management techniques and derivatives such as options . The trade-off is that these active ETFs can be more complicated and expensive than their plain-vanilla counterparts.

Tax efficiency also depends on your circumstances and your financial goals , meaning the fund with the lowest apparent tax burden isn't necessarily the best choice for all investors.

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.
